topic: Search, question answering, summarisation and patient timelines over medical records
summary: Search by meaning solves the synonym problem that keyword search has, but keyword search stays better for drug names, and the combination is best. Chart question answering is in routine use at some US hospitals; a small randomised trial of a tool that cites every claim saved 37.6% of task time. A larger randomised trial of automatic chart summaries in real use found less perceived load, no time saved and falling use. Summaries contain errors at a level similar to or above physicians, omissions are more frequent than hallucinations, and timing is a recurrent weakness. Evidence on German hospital records is thin, and no study found measures time saved by AI-generated patient timelines.

findings.claim: Where a chart search exists, most physicians use it, and they mainly type short clinical terms.
findings.detail: Kaiser Permanente Northern California, April 2018 to May 2019, 4,328,330 searches by 34,735 users, 208,374 unique terms. 75.6% of physicians searched at least once. Top terms were statin, colonoscopy and pft, each under 2% of searches.
findings.source: Ruppel et al., Assessment of EHR Search Patterns and Practices, JAMA Network Open
findings.talk_use: Shows that people come to the record with questions, and which ones.

findings.claim: Suggesting medical synonyms improves chart search, because users do not think of the other terms themselves.
findings.detail: 33 clinicians and staff ran simulated search tasks with and without automatic query suggestions based on UMLS and search logs. Performance was rated higher with suggestions. Ratings are subjective, with no gold standard.
findings.quote: in most cases the participants had not thought of these terms on their own
findings.source: Hanauer et al., Semantically-based query recommendation for an EHR search engine, J Biomed Inform
findings.talk_use: Motivates semantic search: the searcher does not know how the author phrased it.

findings.claim: In one patient's discharge summary, keyword search works well for identical words but drops by almost half for synonyms, while embedding search stays stable.
findings.detail: CliniQ: 1,000 MIMIC-III discharge summaries, 1,246 queries, 77,206 relevance judgments. Mean reciprocal rank x 100 for synonyms: BM25 44.8, BM25 with UMLS synonyms 53.1, best embedding 84.3, hybrid 85.0; for identical words 83.9, 83.9, 87.7, 94.3. English intensive-care data; public benchmark, preprint.
findings.quote: BM25 presents strong capacities in string match, achieving an MRR of over 80%, but it struggles in semantic matching.
findings.source: Zhao et al., CliniQ, arXiv 2502.06252
findings.talk_use: Bar chart keyword vs embedding by match type, with examples RA / rheumatoid arthritis and amlodipine / hypertension.

findings.claim: For drug names across many patients, plain keyword search ranked first, and the combination of keyword and embedding search was best overall.
findings.detail: Same benchmark, multi-patient setting. Overall MRR x 100: hybrid 67.0, best embedding 60.4, BM25 59.2. For drug queries BM25 beat every other method on the top-of-list metrics. Embedding models made for biomedicine were generally weaker than general ones.
findings.quote: Dense retrievers behave suboptimally in drug retrieval under Multi-Patient setting
findings.source: Zhao et al., CliniQ, arXiv 2502.06252
findings.talk_use: Counter-evidence slide or Q&A: new methods add to keyword search and do not replace it.

findings.claim: A children's hospital made 166 million notes searchable by meaning, in under a second and for about 4,000 US dollars per month.
findings.detail: Philadelphia, 1.68 million patients. Five clinicians, three abstraction tasks, median time per patient 40 to 30 s, 67 to 32 s and 260 to 28 s compared with keyword-based chart review. The last task compared unlike procedures by the authors' own account. Main errors were temporal, because no date filter was set.
findings.quote: keyword search fails on synonyms, abbreviations, negations, and paraphrases
findings.source: Mutinda et al., Health System Scale Semantic Search Across Unstructured Clinical Notes, arXiv 2604.25605
findings.talk_use: Shows feasibility at hospital scale and low running cost, with research use in mind.

findings.claim: Semantic search over notes found more patients with confirmed genetic disease than diagnosis codes could ever find.
findings.detail: 71 cohorts, 812 confirmed patients. Semantic search reached 97.4% within 1,000 candidates and 98.5% within 10,000; having any relevant code at any depth covered at most 75.0%. At cohort size, recall was only 27.6% (codes 20.3%), and precision could not be estimated, so manual review is still needed.
findings.number: 97.4% within 1,000 candidates vs at most 75.0% with codes
findings.source: Mutinda et al., arXiv 2604.25605
findings.talk_use: Cohort finding for research: information sits in text, beyond billing codes.

findings.claim: Training a search model on German hospital documents from Essen nearly doubled a retrieval score, but answers about single patients hardly improved.
findings.detail: About 11 million synthetic question-answer pairs from 400,000 documents of 163,840 patients. mAP@100 0.27 versus 0.14 (multilingual-e5) and 0.11 (bge-m3). Patient-centred BERTScore F1 0.781 versus 0.778. One site, no comparison with keyword search, no unanswerable questions, 27-51% of synthetic pairs filtered out.
findings.source: Arzideh et al., Improving RAG for Health Care by Fine-Tuning Clinical Embedding Models, JMIR
findings.talk_use: German-language evidence from a university hospital in the same state as UKM.

findings.claim: One symptom has many names: a German medical lexicon lists Atemnot, Kurzatmigkeit, dyspnea, shortness of breath and SOB under one entry.
findings.detail: DocCheck Flexikon entry Dyspnoe, ICD-10 R06.0. Useful for explaining embeddings: keyword search compares letters, an embedding puts similar meanings close together on a map. The lexicon does not list Luftnot in what was read.
findings.source: DocCheck Flexikon, Dyspnoe
findings.talk_use: Intuition slide for embeddings and semantic search.

findings.claim: Search by meaning often confuses a finding with its absence.
findings.detail: Dense retrieval on biomedical literature: contradiction detection MRR 0.023, and a keyword-based design worked better. A separate reproduction of the NevIR benchmark (arXiv 2502.13506) reports most models at or below random. Neither used hospital notes; in the Philadelphia study retrieval plus LLM answered 93.9% of 98 negative questions correctly.
findings.quote: Semantic Collapse, where negation signals become indistinguishable in vector space
findings.source: Negation is Not Semantic, arXiv 2603.17580
findings.talk_use: Simple limit to explain: 'effusion' and 'no effusion' are neighbours on the map.

findings.claim: Letting the model write a database query instead of reading the whole record cut the text volume 391-fold and reduced failures, but accuracy stayed below 42%.
findings.detail: FHIRPath-QA, 100 MIMIC-IV demo patients, 2,095 questions. o4-mini tokens per question 629,839 versus 1,609, failures 0.36 versus 0.09 on clinician wording. Where reading did not fail it was more accurate (0.51 versus 0.39). Template questions; the figures differ in places between text and tables for fine-tuned models.
findings.source: FHIRPath-QA, arXiv 2602.23479
findings.talk_use: Q&A: why structured data still matters, and why neither way is solved.

findings.claim: Stanford's chart chat produced on average 2.33 unsupported claims per summary in routine use.
findings.detail: September to December 2025, 16,427 conversations, 719 sampled summaries: 0.73 hallucinations and 1.60 inaccuracies each, half with zero or one unsupported claim. Measured by an automated method adapted from VeriFact. Manual review in the pilot found errors in temporal order, numbers, roles and inferred plans.
findings.quote: there were an average of 2.33 unsupported claims
findings.source: Shah et al. (Stanford), Adoption and Use of LLMs at an Academic Medical Center, arXiv 2602.00074
findings.talk_use: Argument for the chain of proof: even a well-run system needs source checks.

findings.claim: Within three months of launch, 1,075 trained users ran 23,000 chart-chat sessions at Stanford, with diagnostic radiology among the heaviest users.
findings.detail: Most answers returned in under 20 seconds, average LLM cost $0.16 per query, about 75% single-turn sessions. The savings figure for the chat rests on an assumed 10 minutes per query. Links from each fact to its exact source were a planned enhancement.
findings.source: Shah et al. (Stanford), arXiv 2602.00074
findings.talk_use: Demand is real; radiology link; warning that users may stop checking.

findings.claim: In a randomised crossover trial, a chart search tool that cites every claim cut task time by 37.6% without lowering quality.
findings.detail: Duke, 20 participants, 200 structured cases, seven specialties, blinded expert rating: 9.67 to 6.03 minutes. Participants rated their own performance slightly worse with the tool. Single site, one evaluator per use case who also wrote the cases; preprint.
findings.quote: Each response includes citations linking each claim to the original data source
findings.source: Gao et al., A Randomized Controlled Trial and Pilot of Scout, arXiv 2604.26953
findings.talk_use: Closest trial evidence for the chain-of-proof idea: work shifts from searching to verifying.

findings.claim: An automated checker flagged 17 of 187 claims as unsupported, but 11 of these were in fact supported by the chart.
findings.detail: Manual check of five patient outputs at Duke. All 170 claims marked as supported were confirmed. The remaining six were mainly outdated or misclassified facts, two of them correct but not properly cited. Very small sample.
findings.source: Gao et al., arXiv 2604.26953
findings.talk_use: Q&A: can an AI check the AI? Useful as a filter, humans still decide.

findings.claim: Open models running fully offline answered questions on Finnish oncology records with 95.3% accuracy, with clinically significant errors in 2.9% of outputs.
findings.detail: 1,664 expert-annotated question-answer pairs, 183 patients, models up to 70B parameters; quantised versions did equally well. In 0.96% of cases a rewording turned a correct answer into a clinically significant error. Predefined answer options, one region, one reviewer.
findings.source: Saukkoriipi et al., Automating Clinical Information Retrieval from Finnish EHRs, arXiv 2603.26434
findings.talk_use: Shows that on-premises models work for a small European language.

findings.claim: Giving a model only the retrieved passages came close to giving it the whole hospital stay, but missed a third of antibiotics when few passages were used.
findings.detail: 200 hospitalisations per task, mean 74k to 108k tokens, three models. Retrieval clearly beat recent notes for imaging procedures and showed no consistent gain for diagnosis lists. With 20 passages 32% of antibiotics were missed; for 22.4% the notes did not contain the needed information.
findings.quote: RAG closely matches or exceeds the performance of using recent notes, and approaches the performance of using the models' full context
findings.source: Myers et al., Evaluating RAG vs. Long-Context Input for Clinical Reasoning over EHRs, arXiv 2508.14817
findings.talk_use: Q&A: why not give the whole record to the model? And: what is not documented cannot be found.

findings.claim: Tests of chart question answering look mostly at recent events; on questions spread over the whole history, 7-8B models scored about 58-67%.
findings.detail: 55.3% of MedAlign instructions concern the last quarter of the patient timeline. TIMER-Bench spreads evidence over time; general instruction-tuned models scored 57.96% and 67.41% for correctness. Benchmark written and judged by language models; single centre.
findings.source: Cui et al., TIMER, arXiv 2503.04176
findings.talk_use: Caveat for the ten-year overview: long histories are the hard case.

findings.claim: In a randomised trial of Epic's outpatient chart summary, clinicians felt less load but saved no charting time, and use fell within three months.
findings.detail: 284 clinicians, 42 specialties, 90 days in 2026, 74,474 summaries, 14.2% interacted with. Task load -27.4 on a 0-400 scale (P=0.02), charting time -1.2 s per encounter (95% CI -19.0 to 16.6), interaction 21.5% to 10.5%, net promoter score -22. No safety events reported. Preprint.
findings.source: Chin et al., A Pragmatic Randomized Trial of an EHR-Integrated Generative AI Chart Summarization Tool, medRxiv 2026.08.26.26361496
findings.talk_use: Honest counter-evidence: a generic summary nobody asked for does not save time.

findings.claim: For short clinical texts, summaries from the best adapted language model were rated equal to (45%) or better than (36%) those of medical experts.
findings.detail: Ten physicians, reader study on radiology reports, patient questions and progress notes. Hallucinations 5% (model) versus 12% (experts). Not long, multi-year charts; pre-2024 models.
findings.quote: majority of cases, summaries from our best adapted LLMs are either equivalent (45%) or superior (36%)
findings.source: Van Veen et al., Adapted LLMs can outperform medical experts in clinical text summarization, Nature Medicine
findings.talk_use: Shows potential, with the limit that these were short texts.

findings.claim: In daily use at Stanford, 2 of 100 reviewed AI hospital-course summaries had hallucinations but 25 had omissions.
findings.detail: Single-arm pilot, 384 discharges, 11 physicians, AI text used in 57%. Inaccuracies 20, wrong citations 0, no severe harm. Documentation time change not significant (P=.13), although 67% of responses perceived savings.
findings.source: Grolleau et al., Physician-Reported Safety Outcomes of AI-Generated Hospital Course Summaries, JAMA Network Open
findings.talk_use: Key trust point: what is missing is the larger problem, and source links do not reveal it.

findings.claim: In a blinded comparison, AI discharge narratives had more errors than those of physicians (2.91 versus 1.82 each), with low overall harm.
findings.detail: 100 hospital stays of 3 to 6 days, 22 attending reviewers, quality and preference similar. AI text more concise and coherent, less comprehensive. Harm score 0.84 versus 0.36 on 0-7. Older model generation.
findings.source: Williams et al., Physician- and LLM-Generated Hospital Discharge Summaries, JAMA Internal Medicine
findings.talk_use: Balances Van Veen; physicians make errors too.

findings.claim: In a Dutch hospital, reviewers fully trusted 85.3% of AI discharge summaries and 95.5% of those written by physicians.
findings.detail: 292 paired summaries, 8 blinded clinicians, EHR-integrated tool. AI summaries less complete, more concise, similarly correct, total score equal; 3.1% rejected.
findings.source: Mehri et al., Assessing the quality of AI-generated and physician-written discharge summaries, EBioMedicine
findings.talk_use: European evidence close to the German setting.

findings.claim: A one-screen timeline of the patient record that leads directly to the underlying data was already proposed in the 1990s.
findings.detail: LifeLines, University of Maryland, shown at CHI 1996 for personal histories and at AMIA 1998 for patient records. A descriptive system paper; the project page gives no quantitative results.
findings.quote: The visual display acts as a giant menu, giving direct access to the data.
findings.source: Plaisant et al., LifeLines: using visualization to enhance navigation and analysis of patient records, AMIA
findings.talk_use: Historic picture: the idea is old; what is new is that text can fill it.

findings.claim: Lawrence Weed argued in 1968 for ordering the record by patient problems; this introduced the problem list to a wide audience.
findings.detail: NEJM 1968;278:593-600. The original text was not read here, only the citation and secondary accounts. An early electronic implementation (PROMIS) followed.
findings.source: Weed, Medical records that guide and teach, NEJM
findings.talk_use: Historic counterpoint to document-centred records; cite without quoting.

findings.claim: When lab values and drugs were grouped by problem, users were faster (173 versus 205 s) and made fewer errors (3.4% versus 7.7%).
findings.detail: Randomised block design in an EHR simulation with simple retrieval tasks; also better usability (58.5 versus 41.3) and lower workload. Rule-based grouping without a language model.
findings.source: Semanik et al., Impact of a problem-oriented view on clinical data retrieval, JAMIA
findings.talk_use: Evidence that overview organised by question helps, independent of AI.

findings.claim: Language models can rebuild a timeline from case reports: GPT-5 found 93% of events with a mean time error of 4 hours, a 70B open model 76% and 24 hours.
findings.detail: 40 sepsis case reports annotated by clinicians; order concordance 0.965 and 0.908. Errors are mostly wrong timing. Case reports are tidier than hospital charts, and the authors say it is not ready for clinical deployment.
findings.source: Noroozizadeh and Weiss, sepsis textual time series, arXiv 2504.12326
findings.talk_use: Status of automatic patient timelines, and the gap between open and commercial models.

findings.claim: A Stanford before-after study reports that median CT/MRI review time fell from 11.3 to 9.4 minutes after an AI chart summary was introduced.
findings.detail: Epic Imaging Insights, over 133,000 exams, no control group. Of 102 summaries, completeness met expectations in 70%. Conference abstract scheduled for RSNA on 2 December 2026, after the date of this report; page could not be opened.
findings.source: AuntMinnie, RSNA 2026 preview
findings.talk_use: Only for Q&A, with the caveat that it is an unpublished, uncontrolled result.

caveats: Time savings differ by design: 37.6% in set tasks, none in a pragmatic trial, 17% in an uncontrolled radiology study. The explanation that concrete questions gain more than unrequested summaries is an inference.
ChatEHR savings ($2.2 million for the chat, $6 million overall) are estimates; the chat figure assumes 10 minutes saved per query.
Error rates use different units (claims per summary, share of summaries, share of outputs) and must not be shown on one axis.
Many key items are preprints, several read as abstract only.
Almost all data are English; intensive-care data from MIMIC dominate the benchmarks.
Source links do not reveal omissions, which were more frequent than hallucinations in MedAgentBrief (25 versus 2 of 100).
gaps: No study found on semantic search over patient records in ORBIS or another German hospital system; no keyword comparison on German notes.
No measured evidence that AI-generated timelines save clinician time; trials of interactive timelines were not searched because the shared search budget ran out.
Automation bias with cited summaries was not searched.
EHRSQL, EHRNoteQA and LongHealth were not read; no independent accuracy data for Epic's chat assistant found.
Weed 1968 full text not read; Luftnot not verified as a listed synonym.
Stony Brook paper (npj Digital Medicine 10.1038/s41746-026-03320-y) known only from a news report.
